readings.c1s4:
¶
{{smaller block|During this parley the insurgents had made themselves masters of the West Port, rushing upon the ''Waiters'' (so the people were called who had the charge of the gates), and possessing themselves of the keys.
{{right|''Scott'', Heart of Mid-Lothian, vi.}}}}

'''3.''' One who waits; one who abides in expectation of the happening of some event, the arrival of some appointed time, some opportunity, or the like.
readings.c2s3:
¶
{{smaller|'''Lords''' or '''grooms in waiting''', officers of the British royal household who hold the same position under a queen regnant as lords or grooms of the bedchamber under a king. ''Encyc. Brit.'', XXI. 37.}}

'''waitingly''' (wā′ting-li), ''adv.'' By waiting; as if waiting.

'''waiting-maid''' (wā′ting-mād), ''n.'' A maid-servant; a waiting-woman.
{{smaller block|<poem>Tokens for a ''waiting-maid''
To trim the butler with.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher (and another)'', Love’s Cure, ii. 2.}}}}

'''waiting-room''' (wā′ting-röm), ''n.'' A room for the use of persons waiting, as at a railway-station or a public office.
{{smaller block|A motley crowd filled the restaurant and ''waiting-rooms.''
{{right|''Harper’s Mag.'', LXXIX. 670.}}}}

'''waiting-vassal†''' (wā′ting-vas″a̤l), ''n.'' An attendant.
{{smaller block|Your carters or your ''waiting-vassals.''
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., ii. 1. 121.}}}}

'''waiting-woman''' (wā′ting-wu̇m″a̤n), ''n.'' A woman who attends or waits in service; a waiting-maid.
{{smaller block|Chambermaids and ''waiting-women.''
{{right|''Shak.'', Lear, iv. 1. 65.}}}}

'''waitress''' (wā′tres), ''n.'' [< ''wait(e)r'' + ''-ess.''] A woman who waits at table: originally used only of one who served in a place of public entertainment.

{{smaller block|''Waive'', a Woman that is Out-law’d; she is so called as being forsaken of the Law, and not an Out-law as a Man is.
{{right|''Glossographia Anglicana'' (1707).}}}}

'''waiver''' (wā′vėr), ''n.'' [Formerly also ''waver''; < OF. *''waiver'', ''weyver'', waive, refuse, renounce, inf. as noun: see ''waive''.] In ''law'': (''a'') The act of waiving; the intentional relinquishment of a known right; the passing by or declining to accept a thing.
{{smaller block|''Waiver'', in a general way, may be said to occur wherever one, in possession of a right conferred either by law or by contract, and knowing the attendant facts, does or forbears to do something inconsistent with the existence of the right or of his intention to rely upon it; in which case he is said to have waived it, and he is estopped from claiming anything by reason of it afterward.
{{right|''Bishop.''}}
The earliest conception . . . of public justice was a solemn ''waiver'' on the part of the community of its right and duty of protection in the case of one who had wronged his fellow-member of the folk.
{{right|''J. R. Green'', Conq. of England, p. 23.}}}}
(''b'') In ''old Eng. law'', the legal process by which a woman was waived, or put out of the protection of the law.

{{RunningHeader|wait|6805|wake}}{{nop}}(''f'') To be ready to serve; do the bidding of. {{smaller block|Yea, let none that ''wait on'' thee be ashamed. {{right|Ps. xxv. 3.}}}} {{smaller block|Therefore turn thou to thy God: keep mercy and judgment, and ''wait on'' thy God continually. {{right|Hos. xii. 6.}}}} (''g'') To attend upon as a servant; act as attendant to; be in the service of. {{smaller block|The Syrians had brought away . . . a little maid: and she ''waited on'' Naaman’s wife. {{right|2 Ki. v. 2.}}}} {{smaller block|How now, Simple! where have you been? I must ''wait on'' myself, must I? {{right|''Shak.'', M. W. of W., i. 1. 208.}}}} (''h'') To go to see; call upon; visit; attend. {{smaller block|I . . . have been twice to ''wait upon'' Dr. Brady; but was both times disappointed. {{right|''Edmond Gibson'' (Ellis’s Lit. Letters, p. 229).}}}} {{smaller block|I suppose he will be here to ''wait on'' Mrs. Malaprop as soon as he is dress’d. {{right|''Sheridan'', The Rivals, i. 2.}}}} (''i'') To escort; accompany; attend; specifically, to attend as bridesmaid or groomsman. [Colloq.] {{smaller block|Gentlemen, I beg pardon — I must ''wait on'' you down stairs; here is a person come on particular business. {{right|''Sheridan'', School for Scandal, iv. 3.}}}} {{smaller block|I used to be ''waitin’ on'' her to singin’ school. {{right|''H. B. Stowe'', Oldtown Stories, p. 123.}}}} (''j'') To attend or follow as a consequence; be associated with; accompany. {{smaller block|Now, good digestion ''wait on'' appetite, And health on both! ''Shak.'', Macbeth, iii. 4. 38. Such silence ''waits on'' Philomela’s strains. {{right|''Pope'', Winter, l. 78.}}}} {{smaller block|Yet a rich guerdon ''waits on'' minds that dare, If aught be in them of immortal seed. {{right|''Wordsworth'', Sonnets, ii. 4.}}}} '''To wait on.'''   [''On'', adv.]   In ''falconry'', to fly or hover aloft, waiting for game to be sprung: said of a hawk. {{smaller block|When the hawk has taken two or three pigeons in this way, and mounts immediately in expectation—in short, begins to ''wait on''—she should . . . be tried at game. {{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', IX. 9.}}}} '''II.''' ''trans.'' '''1†.''' To observe; examine; take notice of; expect; watch for; look out for. {{smaller block|Nyght and day he spedde him that he can, To ''wayten'' a tyme of his conclusioun. {{right|''Chaucer'', Franklin’s Tale, l. 535.}}}} {{smaller block|''Waite'' what y dide to marie maudeleyne, And what y seide to thomas of ynde. {{right|''Political Poems'', etc. (ed. Furnivall), p. 165.}}}} '''2†.''' To plan; scheme; contrive. {{smaller block|& [he] thouȝt or he went a-way he wold ȝif he miȝt ''wayte'' hire sum wicked torn what bi-tidde after. {{right|''William of Palerne'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 148.}}}} '''3†.''' To seek. {{smaller block|Than farde Nectanabus forthe fro that place; Hee wendes too a wildernes & ''waites'' him erbes. {{right|''Alisaunder of Macedoine'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 808.}}}} '''4.''' To stay for; attend; await; expect. {{smaller block|Go ''wait'' me in the gallery. {{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Maid’s Tragedy, iv. 1.}}}} {{smaller block| They all Complain aloud of Cato’s discipline, And ''wait'' but the command to change their master. {{right|''Addison'', Cato, i. 3.}}}} {{smaller block|Then let him receive the new knowledge and ''wait'' us,
Pardoned in Heaven. {{right|''Browning'', Lost Leader.}}}} '''5.''' To defer; put off; keep waiting: said of a meal. [Colloq.] {{smaller block|I shall go for a walk; don’t you and Herbert ''wait'' supper for me. {{right|''T. Hughes'', Tom Brown at Rugby, ii. 9.}}}} '''6†.''' To attend upon; accompany; escort. {{smaller block|Most noble consul! let us ''wait'' him home. {{right|''B. Jonson'', Catiline, iii. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|Proffering the Hind to ''wait'' her half the way; That, since the sky was clear, an hour of talk Might help her to beguile the tedious walk. {{right|''Dryden'', Hind and Panther, i. 557.}}}} '''7†.''' To follow as a consequence of something; attend upon. {{smaller block|Such doom ''Waits'' luxury and lawless care of gain! {{right|''J. Philips'', Cider, i.}}}} {{smaller block|Defend me from the Woes which Mortals ''wait.'' {{right|''Congreve'', Hymn to Venus.}}}} '''To wait attendance†''', {{smaller|to remain in attendance; be on hand or within call.}} {{smaller block|''Wait attendance'' Till you hear further from me. {{right|''Shak.'', T. of A., i. 1. 161.}}}} '''wait-a-bit thorn.''' See under ''thorn.'' '''waiter''' (wā′tėr), ''n.''   [< ME. ''waitere'', ''wayter'', ''weyter'', later ''watare'', < OF. ''waitier'', ''guetteur'', etc., ''guetter'', F. ''guetter'', wait: see ''wait'', ''v.'' Cf. MHG. ''wahtære'', ''wehter'', G. ''wächter'', a watchman.]   '''1†.''' A watcher. {{smaller block|And the childe ''weyter'' heuede vp his eyen, and bihelde. {{right|''Wyclif'', 2 Ki. [2 Sam.] xiii. 34.}}}} '''2†.''' A watchman; a guard or keeper. {{smaller block|During this parley the insurgents had made themselves masters of the West Port, rushing upon the ''Waiters'' (so the people were called who had the charge of the gates), and possessing themselves of the keys. {{right|''Scott'', Heart of Mid-Lothian, vi.}}}} '''3.''' One who waits; one who abides in expectation of the happening of some event, the arrival of some appointed time, some opportunity, or the like. {{smaller block|''Waiters'' on Providence. {{right|''Disraeli'', Coningsby, ii. 4.}}}} '''4.''' A domestic servant. {{smaller|Specifically—(''a''†) A man-servant for rough work about a house.}} {{smaller block|Dayly iiii other of these gromes, called ''wayters'', to make fyres, to sett up tressyls and bourdes, with yomen of chambre, and to help dresse the beddes of sylke and arras. {{right|Quoted in ''Babees Book'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 314.}}}} {{smaller|(''b''†) A waiting-woman.}} {{smaller block|Enter . . . two waiting-women. . . . Bid your ''waiters'' Stand further off, and I’ll come nearer to you. {{right|''Massinger'', Unnatural Combat, i. 1.}}}} {{smaller|(''c'') A man-servant who waits at table: applied more commonly to those who serve in hotels or restaurants.}} {{smaller block|Enter ''waiter.'' ''Wait.'' Here is a gentleman desires to speak with Mr. Vincent. ''Vin.'' I come. [Exit Vincent with ''Waiter.'' {{right|''Wycherley'', Love in a Wood, i. 2.}}}} {{smaller block|Head-''waiter'' of the chop-house here, To which I most resort. {{right|''Tennyson'', Will Waterproof.}}}} '''5.''' An officer in the employ of the British custom-house. See ''coast-waiter'', ''tide-waiter''.—'''6.''' A tray; a salver. {{smaller block|Just then a servant brought Lady Louisa a note upon a ''waiter'', which is a ceremony always used to her ladyship. {{right|''Miss Burney'', Evelina, lxxviii.}}}} {{smaller block|Ezra came quietly into the room again, and took up the ''waiter'' with the jelly-glass and the napkin. {{right|''The Century'', XLI. 584.}}}} {{smaller|'''Minority waiter''', a waiter out of employment: in humorous allusion to a political minority, as being out of office. Compare def. 3.}} {{smaller block|I told Thomas that your Honour had already inlisted five disbanded chairmen, seven ''minority waiters'', and thirteen billiard-markers. {{right|''Sheridan'', The Rivals, ii. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|'''Quarterly waiter.''' Same as ''quarter-waiter.''—'''Waiters’ cramp,''' an occupation neurosis of public waiters, consisting in pain and muscular spasm, excited by the attempt to carry dishes in the customary manner.}} '''waiterage''' (wā′tėr-ạ̄j), ''n.''   [< ''waiter'' + ''-age.'']   Attendance by a waiter; service. {{smaller block|Imperial-Hotel people . . . had brightened up; . . . all was done for me then that human ''waiterage'' in the circumstances could do. {{right|''Carlyle'', The Century, XXIV. 23.}}}} '''waitering''' (wā′tėr-ing), ''n.''   [< ''waiter'' + ''-ing''1.]   The employment or duties of a waiter. {{smaller block|Nor yet can you lay down the gentleman’s-service . . . and take up ''Waitering.'' {{right|''Dickens'', Somebody’s Luggage, i.}}}} '''wait-fee''' (wāt′fē), ''n.'' In ''feudal law'', a periodical payment by way of commutation for relief from the duty of maintaining a tower and performing guard on the wall of a royal castle. '''waiting''' (wā′ting), ''n.''   [< ME. ''waitynge, waytynge;'' verbal n. of ''wait, v.'']   '''1†.''' Watching; hence, an ogling. {{smaller block|Al the lordshep of lecherye in lengthe and in brede, As in workes and in wordes and ''waitynges'' of eyes. {{right|''Piers Plowman'' (C), iii. 94.}}}} '''2.''' The act of staying or remaining in expectation. {{smaller block|In all ages, men have fought over words, without ''waiting'' to know what the words really signified. {{right|''J. Fiske'', Cosmic Philos., I. 122.}}}} {{smaller block|There was an awful ''waiting'' in the earth, As if a mystery greatened to its birth. {{right|''R. W. Gilder'', Interlude.}}}} '''3.''' Attendance; service. {{smaller block|Green glasses for hock, and excellent ''waiting'' at table. {{right|''George Eliot'', Middlemarch, xxxvi.}}}} {{smaller|'''Lords''' or '''grooms in waiting''', officers of the British royal household who hold the same position under a queen regnant as lords or grooms of the bedchamber under a king. ''Encyc. Brit.'', XXI. 37.}} '''waitingly''' (wā′ting-li), ''adv.'' By waiting; as if waiting. '''waiting-maid''' (wā′ting-mād), ''n.'' A maid-servant; a waiting-woman. {{smaller block|Tokens for a ''waiting-maid'' To trim the butler with. {{right|''Fletcher (and another)'', Love’s Cure, ii. 2.}}}} '''waiting-room''' (wā′ting-röm), ''n.'' A room for the use of persons waiting, as at a railway-station or a public office. {{smaller block|A motley crowd filled the restaurant and ''waiting-rooms.'' {{right|''Harper’s Mag.'', LXXIX. 670.}}}} '''waiting-vassal†''' (wā′ting-vas″a̤l), ''n.'' An attendant. {{smaller block|Your carters or your ''waiting-vassals.'' {{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., ii. 1. 121.}}}} '''waiting-woman''' (wā′ting-wu̇m″a̤n), ''n.'' A woman who attends or waits in service; a waiting-maid. {{smaller block|Chambermaids and ''waiting-women.'' {{right|''Shak.'', Lear, iv. 1. 65.}}}} '''waitress''' (wā′tres), ''n.''   [< ''wait(e)r'' + ''-ess.'']   A woman who waits at table: originally used only of one who served in a place of public entertainment. {{smaller block|The curtain drew up, and we beheld, seated at a long table, a company of monkeys! . . . the waiter and ''waitress'' were monkeys. {{right|''Anna Mary Howitt'', Art Student in Munich, xviii.}}}} '''wait-service''' (wāt′sėr″vis), ''n.'' The act of serving as wait or ward of a castle.—{{smaller|'''Tenure of wait-service''', the holding a virgate or yard-land in consideration of serving as castle-wait or watch.}} '''wait-treble''' (wāt′treb″l), ''n.'' A sort of bagpipe. ''Halliwell.'' '''waive''' (wāv), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''waived'', ppr. ''waiving''.   [Also ''wave''; < ME. ''waiven'', ''wayven'', ''weiven'', ''weyven'', < OF. *''waiver'', *''weiver'', ''weyver'', ''guesver'', ''guever'' (ML. ''waviare''), waive, refuse, abandon, give over, surrender, give back, resign, perhaps < Icel. ''veifa'', vibrate swing about, move to and fro, = Norw. ''veiva'', swing about, = OHG. ''weibōn'', MHG. ''weiben'', ''waiben'', fluctuate, waver, = Goth. ''bi-waibjan'', waver; cf. L. ''vibrare'', vibrate. Cf. ''waif'', ''n.'' The verb ''waive'' is distinct from ''wave''1, with which it is often confounded.]   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1†.''' To refuse; forsake; decline; shun. {{smaller block|Anoñ he ''weyveth'' milk and flessh and al, And every deyntee that is in that hous. {{right|''Chaucer'', Manciple’s Tale, l. 159.}}}} {{smaller block|Within two daies after wee were hailed by two West-Indies men; but when they saw vs ''waife'' them for the King of France, they gaue vs their broad sides. {{right|''Capt. John Smith'', Works, II. 211.}}}} {{smaller block|He lent you imprest money, and upbraids it; Furnished you for the wooing, and now ''waives'' you. {{right|''B. Jonson'', Magnetick Lady, iv. 1.}}}} '''2†.''' To move; remove; push aside. {{smaller block|Biddeth Amende-ȝow meke him til his maistre ones, To ''wayue'' vp the wiket that the womman shette, Tho [when] Adam and Eue eten apples vnrosted. {{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), v. 611.}}}} {{smaller block|Thou, by whom he was deceived Of love, and from his purpose ''weived''. {{right|''Gower'', Conf. Amant., ii.}}}} '''3.''' To relinquish; forsake; forbear to insist on or claim; defer for the present; forgo: as, to ''waive'' a subject; to ''waive'' a claim or privilege. {{smaller block|Whereas it hath pleased the Heads of the University to understand it for three years absolutely, I purpose not to ''wave'' that construction. {{right|''Thomas Adams'' (Ellis’s Lit. Letters, p. 147).}}}} {{smaller block|You may safely ''wave'' the nobility of your birth, and rely on your actions for your fame. {{right|''Dryden'', Ded. of Plutarch’s Lives.}}}} {{smaller block|I have so great a love for you that I can ''waive'' opportunities of gain to help you. {{right|''Steele'', Spectator, No. 456.}}}} {{smaller block|I have ''waived'' his visit till I am in town. {{right|''Walpole'', Letters, II. 184.}}}} '''4.''' In ''law'': (''a'') To relinquish intentionally (a known right), or intentionally to do an act inconsistent with claiming (it). See ''waiver''. (''b'') To throw away, as a thief stolen goods in his flight. (''c'') In ''old Eng. law'', to put out of the protection of the law, as a woman. {{smaller block|If the defendant be a woman, the proceeding is called a waver; for, as women were not sworn to the law, . . . they could not properly be outlawed, but were said to be ''waived'', i. e., derelicta, left out, or not regarded. {{right|''Wharton.''}}}} '''II.''' ''intrans.'' To depart; deviate.
